sourceObjects.label: sales
sourceObjects.description: The transaction header for the whole domain: totals, tax, discounts, cost of goods, and every foreign key that gives a sale its who/where/when. This is the source of truth for revenue, margin and ticket counts at sale grain. It is NOT a takings/cash table (that is ls_sale_payments), NOT a product table (that is ls_sale_lines), and it contains open shopping carts and voided tickets that must be filtered out before any money question.
sourceObjects.grain: one row per Sale record — one register ticket/transaction, in any state (open, completed, voided, archived). Refunds are NOT a separate resource: a refund is a Sale whose lines carry negative unitQuantity and whose payments carry negative amount, so it is also one row here.

fields.name: sale_id
fields.description: Immutable numeric ticket id, unique within the account. The join key for every child table (lines, payments, voids, CC charges, ShipTo, quotes). NOT the human receipt number the customer sees — the Refund endpoint accepts a ticketNumber in its URL path, but no ticketNumber field is published on this object.

fields.name: completed
fields.description: True once the ticket was finalised: inventory has been deducted and payments sum to the total. False = an open/parked ticket sitting on a register (or the working sale behind a saved quote) with NO payments at all. Almost every money question must filter completed = true; omitting it silently mixes unpaid shopping carts into revenue.

Summing without voided = false inflates revenue by the value of every reversed ticket.

sourceObjects.label: sale lines
sourceObjects.description: The product-level truth for the domain: units, per-product revenue, per-line discounts and per-line cost basis. Every product ranking, sell-through, return-rate and item-margin question belongs here, never on the sale header or the item catalogue. It is NOT a tax table (rates are line-level but tax categories live in the org domain) and it carries NO completed/voided flag of its own — those must be joined from ls_sales.
sourceObjects.grain: one row per SaleLine — one charge on one sale. That is a catalog item line, a miscellaneous/non-inventory charge, an item-fee surcharge line, or a refund line (negative unitQuantity). Layaway, special-order and workorder lines share this same grain.

sourceObjects.label: assets

sourceObjects.label: credit notes
sourceObjects.description: Negative-document header mirroring xero_invoices: ACCRECCREDIT reduces what a customer owes (contra revenue), ACCPAYCREDIT reduces what the org owes a supplier (contra spend). Credit is consumed two ways: allocation against invoices (xero_credit_note_allocations) or cash refund (rows in xero_payments); remaining_credit is what is still unconsumed right now.

sourceObjects.label: expense claim payments
sourceObjects.description: Reimbursement cash events, exploded from the Payments array embedded in each expense claim. This is their only home in the design: a Payment served by GET /Payments allocates to exactly one invoice, credit note, prepayment or overpayment, and an expense claim is none of those — so these rows reach staging through the claim scan alone, and a 'total cash paid out' built from xero_payments by itself omits employee reimbursements. Amounts are in org base currency (classic claims carry no currency or rate fields). Status DELETED un-pays the claim yet remains in the payload — filter AUTHORISED on every sum.

sourceObjects.label: file associations
sourceObjects.description: The bridge that turns the file library into audit evidence: each row attaches one file to one business record, addressed by the polymorphic (object_group, object_id) pair. This is how 'which invoices have no supporting document' and 'what paperwork backs this bank transaction' resolve — filter object_group first, then join object_id to that group's table. sourceObjects.label: items
sourceObjects.description: The product/service dimension and the only inventory-balance surface in the accounting API. Document lines reference items by user-editable code (item_code), not by uuid — so this table joins to facts through `code`. Sales/purchase details are DEFAULTS offered in the Xero UI, not transacted prices; the transacted price is always unit_amount on the document line. is_tracked_as_inventory gates the stock story: only tracked items carry quantity_on_hand and total_cost_pool (average-cost value of stock), and both are point-in-time snapshots as of the last sync — Xero exposes no stock history. Those two balance columns are why this table is typed last_value_over_time rather than reference: every other column is catalog configuration, but stock value and quantity are as-at balances that may be summed across items and never across time. Items hard-delete: rows vanish from the API and are tombstoned only by full identity scans.
sourceObjects.grain: one product or service item in the org's catalog, identified by ItemID
sourceObjects.additivityAxis: time — quantity_on_hand and total_cost_pool are as-at-last-sync balances overwritten in place, so they may be summed across items but never across syncs, snapshots or periods

sourceObjects.description: Cash application evidence: each row records money moving between a bank/clearing account and exactly one receivable or payable document. views.label: sales
views.description: The transaction header for the whole domain: totals, tax, discounts, cost of goods, and every foreign key that gives a sale its who/where/when. This is the source of truth for revenue, margin and ticket counts at sale grain. It is NOT a takings/cash table (that is ls_sale_payments), NOT a product table (that is ls_sale_lines), and it contains open shopping carts and voided tickets that must be filtered out before any money question.
views.grain: one row per Sale record — one register ticket/transaction, in any state (open, completed, voided, archived). Refunds are NOT a separate resource: a refund is a Sale whose lines carry negative unitQuantity and whose payments carry negative amount, so it is also one row here.

views.label: sale lines
views.description: The product-level truth for the domain: units, per-product revenue, per-line discounts and per-line cost basis. Every product ranking, sell-through, return-rate and item-margin question belongs here, never on the sale header or the item catalogue. It is NOT a tax table (rates are line-level but tax categories live in the org domain) and it carries NO completed/voided flag of its own — those must be joined from ls_sales.
views.grain: one row per SaleLine — one charge on one sale. That is a catalog item line, a miscellaneous/non-inventory charge, an item-fee surcharge line, or a refund line (negative unitQuantity). Layaway, special-order and workorder lines share this same grain.

views.label: sale payments
views.description: How money actually moved: cash, card, gift card, store credit, cheque, on-account. This is the takings/tender-mix table and the cash-reconciliation table. It is NOT revenue: layaway instalments, deposits and on-account payments land on the day the money moved, whereas ls_sales recognises revenue at complete_time. Refund payments appear here as negative amounts.
views.grain: one row per SalePayment — one tender applied to, or refunded from, one sale. A single sale can have many (split tender, layaway instalments); a credit-account deposit is deliberately recorded as TWO rows.

views.label: sale accounts
views.description: The bridge that makes gift cards and store credit interpretable: it ties the negative payment that funded a card to the sale line that sold it and to the CreditAccount that holds the balance. Without it you cannot distinguish a gift-card ISSUE (money in, no revenue) from a gift-card REDEMPTION (a payment on a later sale). It holds no money of its own and must never be aggregated.
views.grain: one row per SaleAccount — one gift-card (CreditAccount) association linking a single SalePayment to the SaleLine that created or funded it. Documented one-to-one with SalePayment, so a payment has zero or one row here.

views.label: sale payment signatures
views.description: Evidence that a customer signed for a payment, stored as a pointer into Lightspeed's image storage service. Used for chargeback defence and audit trails. It is NOT a measure of anything: there is no amount, no sale id and no approval status here, and a signature can exist on a payment that was later archived/reversed.
views.grain: one row per SalePaymentSignature — one captured signature image belonging to one sale payment.

views.label: sale line inventory allocations
views.description: The bridge from a sale line to the specific inventory lots it consumed or reserved. This is what makes a FIFO cost audit reconstructable, and what shows how much stock an open layaway or special order is holding hostage. It is NOT a stock-on-hand table and NOT a general inventory movement log — it only covers allocations tied to sale lines.
views.grain: one row per InventorySale — one allocation of units from ONE inventory lot to ONE sale line. A line that draws from three lots produces three rows.

views.label: sale voids
views.description: The audit trail for voided transactions: who voided what, where, when and why. This is the loss-prevention table. It is NOT the voided state itself — that lives on ls_sales.voided — and it is NOT a money table: the value voided has to be pulled from the parent sale.
views.grain: one row per SaleVoid — one void event recorded against one sale, with the operator's stated reason.

views.label: cc charges
views.description: Gateway-side truth for integrated card payments: what was authorised, captured, declined, voided or refunded, and the reference ids needed to reconcile against a processor statement. It is NOT the POS payment record (that is ls_sale_payments) and it is NOT a settled-money table — most rows on a busy account are failures and holds. Empty on any merchant using an external terminal.
views.grain: one row per CCCharge — one credit-card transaction ATTEMPT at the processing gateway, including declines, gateway voids and authorisation-only holds.

views.label: processing fees
views.description: What card acceptance actually costs, per payment, broken into fixed/variable components with interchange and scheme sub-breakdowns. The only place in the API where merchant cost of payment acceptance appears. Only populated for merchants on Lightspeed's integrated payments; empty for anyone on an external terminal. It is NOT a payment table — its `amount` column is a notorious trap.
views.grain: one row per ProcessingFee — one fee record the payment processor assessed against one SalePayment.

views.label: quotes
views.description: The pre-sale pipeline: quotes/invoices staff saved for customers. A deliberately thin resource — it has no customer, no totals and no line detail of its own, all of which live on the sale it points at. It is NOT a conversion log: its sale_id is reassigned on every edit, so conversion must be measured from the other direction (ls_sales.quote_id).
views.grain: one row per Quote — one saved, uncompleted sale held for a customer so it can be reloaded at the register later.

views.label: discounts
views.description: The catalogue of reusable discount rules — their names, amounts/percentages, and what kind of discount they are (price rule, loyalty, or manual discount rule). A row is the RULE, not money given away: actual markdown lives in ls_sales.calc_discount and ls_sale_lines.calc_line_discount, which also include price-rule and manual discounts that carry no rule id.
views.grain: one row per named Discount rule that staff or the system can apply to a sale or a sale line.

views.label: items
views.description: The product master: identity, SKUs/barcodes, categorisation, current price levels, cost basis and the flags that govern tax, discounting and stock behaviour. It answers what the store sells today and at what price and margin. It is NOT a sales ledger (units sold and revenue live on sale lines) and NOT stock (quantities live in ls_item_shops). The 1:1 ItemAttributes and itemECommerce sub-objects are folded in here because they share this grain.
views.grain: one catalogue item — a single sellable SKU. Every colour/size variant of a matrix product is its own row here; the matrix itself is a row in ls_item_matrices.

views.label: item shops
views.description: The current stock position per item per shop: quantity on hand, what is sellable, what is on order, and the reorder thresholds. This is a point-in-time snapshot that the API overwrites in place — it is the source of truth for 'how much do we have RIGHT NOW'. It is NOT a history: 'how much stock did we hold in March' cannot be answered here and belongs to the inventory movement log.
views.grain: one item's stock record at one location; shop_id = 0 is the account-wide aggregate, so use it alone for whole-business stock and only shop_id > 0 for per-shop breakdowns.

views.label: item prices
views.description: Every configured price level for every item: Default, MSRP, Online and any account-defined level. ls_items.price/msrp cover the two everyday cases; this table exists for the rest and for level-versus-level comparisons. It holds CURRENT prices only — there is no price history and no record of what any customer actually paid.
views.grain: one price level amount on one item — the unique key is (item_id, use_type_id), not item_id alone.

views.label: item components
views.description: The bill of materials for box and assembly products — which single items make up a box, and how many of each. It explains where ls_item_shops.component_qoh comes from and lets you cost an assembly from its parts. It is NOT a stock table and NOT a sales table; quantity here is a recipe ratio, never a number of units held.
views.grain: one component line: the link between one assembly/box item and one of the items it is made from.

views.label: item vendor nums
views.description: The cross-reference between the shop's items and the part numbers its suppliers use, with the per-vendor buy cost when vendor-cost functionality is enabled. This is how you turn an item into something orderable from a specific supplier, and how you compare what different suppliers charge for the same item. An item may appear here many times (one row per vendor) even though it has only one default vendor.
views.grain: one vendor-specific SKU: one item as catalogued by one vendor.

views.label: item matrices
views.description: The product-family layer above ls_items: family-level identity, defaults and the attribute set that defines the variant axes. Nothing is ever sold, stocked or priced at this grain — the sellable units are the child rows in ls_items joined by item_matrix_id. Use it to collapse variants into products and to read what the colour/size axes mean.
views.grain: one matrix — one variant family of items (e.g. one jersey that exists in five sizes).

views.label: item attribute sets
views.description: Tiny lookup that names what the attribute1/2/3 slots on items and matrices MEAN — e.g. attribute1 = Color, attribute2 = Size. Without it the variant values are unlabelled strings. Lightspeed restricts the vocabulary to four sets; there are no measures here.
views.grain: one attribute-set definition (the schema of a matrix's variant axes).

views.label: item fees
views.description: The configuration list of fixed-amount surcharges that attach to item categories — tyre recycling levies, e-bike environmental fees and similar. It is CONFIGURATION ONLY: money actually charged appears as its own sale line with lineType 'item_fee' (or 'item_fee_refund'), parented to the item's line via parentSaleLineID. Fee revenue questions belong on sale lines, never here.
views.grain: one configured item fee definition.

views.label: images
views.description: Product photo metadata hosted on Lightspeed's Cloudinary account. Answers image-coverage questions (which products have no photo) and supplies the pieces needed to build a display URL. It stores metadata, not image bytes, and the docs warn the endpoint must not be used as an image host for external websites — traffic is monitored and may be billed.
views.grain: one product image, attached to EITHER an item or a matrix (exactly one of the two).

views.label: serialized
views.description: The register of serialized units: bikes, frames, e-bikes and anything else tracked by serial number. It is the place to answer 'what units does this customer own' and 'who owns serial X'. Rows either link to a catalogue item (sold from stock) or stand alone with a free-text description (a customer's own machine logged at the service desk).
views.grain: one serial-number record — one physical serialized unit, whether it came from stock or was logged as a customer's own property.

views.label: tags
views.description: The list of tags staff can attach to items and matrices for ad-hoc grouping. It is the VOCABULARY only — which items carry which tag is not modellable from the documented surface, because the linking object (TagRelations) has no published field table. Use it to see what labelling conventions the account uses, not to segment products.
views.grain: one tag in the account's tag vocabulary.

views.label: tag groups
views.description: Helper list of the tag groups configured on the account. The docs publish NO field table for this object — the two keys here were harvested from the documented example payload — so it should be treated as low-confidence until probed live. Useful only for interpreting the 'group:value' convention seen in tag names.
views.grain: one tag group name for the account.

views.label: seasons
views.description: Legacy organiser: season labels that older accounts used to group items. Lightspeed has DEPRECATED seasons — the documentation states items are now organised with Categories, Manufacturers and Tags only, with Season and Department removed. Staged solely because ls_items.season_id and ls_item_matrices.season_id still exist and must resolve to something.
views.grain: one season label.

views.label: manufacturers
views.description: The brand list: who MAKES the products. Explicitly distinct from vendors/suppliers, who are who the shop BUYS from — the docs note every item can have one manufacturer but multiple vendors. A dimension table with no measures; brand performance is computed by joining items to sale lines.
views.grain: one manufacturer (brand).

views.label: categories
views.description: The hierarchical category tree used to organise items, structured like a directory. Items attach to exactly one node at ANY depth, and the tree is stored as a nested set (leftNode/rightNode) with a precomputed slash-delimited path. Use full_path_name for rollups; it is the only reliable way to aggregate a whole branch.
views.grain: one category node in the item category tree.

views.label: options
views.description: The account's feature switches as name/value strings. It matters to this domain because account-level settings — not the item record — decide how catalogue numbers must be read (for example whether prices carry tax, or whether vendor-cost functionality is enabled at all). The docs enumerate no option names or values, so any specific key must be discovered from a live response.
views.grain: one account option: a name/value pair the account has turned on.

views.label: price levels
views.description: The definitions behind the price levels that ls_item_prices rows reference: their names, whether they are archived, their type, and the calculation parameters used to derive prices from cost. Configuration only — no amounts live here; the per-item amounts are in ls_item_prices.
views.grain: one price level definition on the account.

views.label: catalog vendor items
views.description: What the shop's suppliers say is available to ORDER: supplier part numbers, tiered costs, bulk price breaks, MSRPs, availability status and supersession. This is the supplier's world, not the shop's — it is neither inventory nor sales, and there is no item_id. Match to the shop's catalogue by barcode or manufacturer part number. A POST here imports an entry and creates a real Item.
views.grain: one product entry in one configured vendor catalogue.

views.label: inventory logs
views.description: The inventory movement ledger: every stock change with why it happened (sale, purchase-order receive, transfer, manual adjustment, stocktake correction, refund, auto-add, bulk import) and who caused it. This is the ONLY dated, historical view of stock movement in the R-Series API and the table to reach for when reconciling 'where did the stock go'. It is read-only and it is NOT a stock-level table: current on-hand lives on ItemShop (ls_inventory in the catalogue domain), and units-sold questions belong on sale lines.
views.grain: one inventory change event — one item's stock level changing in one shop, for one reason, at one moment

views.label: inventory count calcs
views.description: The scoreboard of a stocktake: for each item in a count, what the system thought was on hand (calc_qoh) versus what people physically found (counted_qoh). This is where variance and count-accuracy questions are answered. It is auto-maintained and read-only, it is NOT the individual count entries (ls_inventory_count_items) and it is NOT proof the books were adjusted — only a reconcile moves stock.
views.grain: one item within one inventory count (the system-vs-physical rollup for that item/count pair)

views.label: inventory count items
views.description: The keystroke-level record of a stocktake: each quantity an employee entered, when, for which item. This is the audit trail behind a count and the only place with a real per-entry event time and a named counter. It is NOT the per-item total (that is ls_inventory_count_calcs.counted_qoh) and its quantities are observations, never stock movements.
views.grain: one physical counting act — one item counted once by one employee at one moment (counting the same item three times creates three rows)

views.label: inventory count reconciles
views.description: The posted result of a stocktake: the adjustment actually written to the books for each item, in units and in cost value. This is the financial shrinkage record and the only count table that changes stock. It is NOT the variance measurement (ls_inventory_count_calcs) — a variance can exist forever without a reconcile — and it is irreversible once created.
views.grain: one reconcile posting — one item's stock and cost adjustment applied when a count was reconciled

views.label: transfers
views.description: Transfers of stock between shops: one row per transfer document, carrying whether it has been sent and received, which shops and staff were on each end, and the send/receive dates. TransferFrom and TransferTo are one-to-one sub-records of the same document, so they are flattened here rather than split out. This is the document header only — the items and quantities live on ls_transfer_items, and the actual stock movement lands in ls_inventory_logs.
views.grain: one inter-shop transfer document (header), with its origin-side and destination-side records flattened in

views.label: transfer items
views.description: The lines of an inter-shop transfer: which item, how many were meant to go, how many actually left, how many the destination counted, how many landed, and the cost value on each side. This is where transfer discrepancies and stock-lost-in-transit are found. These are mutable current-state quantities on an open document, not dated movements — the dated version is ls_inventory_logs filtered on transfer_id.
views.grain: one line on one transfer — one item on one inter-shop transfer document

views.label: special orders
views.description: Customer special orders: a customer wants something the shop does not stock, the shop optionally takes a deposit and orders it in. Each row bridges the customer side (sale_line_id) with the supply side (order_line_id for a supplier PO, or transfer_item_id when another shop supplies it), plus the contacted/completed workflow flags. It is NOT a sale (no money or price here) and NOT a purchase order — it is the link record that makes 'who is waiting for what' answerable.
views.grain: one special order — one item a named customer asked the shop to bring in, tracked from the sale line it was raised on to the purchase order line or transfer that fulfils it

views.label: transfer from
views.description: The sending side of a stock transfer. Lightspeed models the two ends of a transfer as separate records rather than as two columns, so this table resolves a transfer to the shop the stock left. It exists purely to complete that join and carries no quantities of its own.
views.grain: one origin record for one stock transfer

views.label: transfer to
views.description: The receiving side of a stock transfer, mirroring ls_transfer_from. Resolves a transfer to the shop that received the stock. Reference-only; quantities live on the transfer item lines.
views.grain: one destination record for one stock transfer

views.label: purchase orders
views.description: One row per PURCHASE ORDER: stock the business is buying from a supplier, with the header-level costs, discounts, currency and lifecycle flags. This is the document the shop sends to a vendor and later checks in against. It is NOT a customer order — customer purchases live in the sales domain (Sale/SaleLine); a customer waiting on an item is a SpecialOrder. It is also NOT a receipt: what physically arrived is in ls_order_shipments / ls_order_shipment_items and in the per-line counters on ls_purchase_order_lines.
views.grain: one purchase order raised with one vendor for one shop (Lightspeed resource `Order`)

views.label: purchase order lines
views.description: One row per item line on a purchase order: which product, how many units were ordered, at what unit cost, and how many of them have physically landed. This is the line-level truth for 'how many X are on order' and for per-product buying history and cost trends. It is NOT a receipt log — the two receiving columns are running counters that are overwritten in place, with no history of when units arrived; dated receipts live in ls_order_shipment_items.
views.grain: one product line on one purchase order (one row per OrderLine)

views.label: order shipments
views.description: One row per delivery received against a purchase order: how many units landed, the landed cost of that delivery, the freight and discount allocated to it, and who received it when. A PO can arrive in several shipments, each with its own sequence number and invoice due date. This is the DATED receiving fact for the purchasing domain; it is NOT the purchase order's own totals (those are on ls_purchase_orders) and it is NOT per-item detail (that is ls_order_shipment_items). The Order-scoped OrderShipment endpoint and the account-wide Shipment endpoint are documented as identical, so they are one table here.
views.grain: one shipment (receiving event) against one purchase order

views.label: order shipment items
views.description: One row per item received in a shipment: how many units of that product landed in that delivery, its cost before freight, its allocated freight and discount, and its final landed cost. This is the finest-grained, dated goods-receipt fact in the purchasing domain and the correct basis for actual landed unit cost. It is NOT the ordered quantity (that is ls_purchase_order_lines.quantity) and it carries no link to the PO line it satisfies — only the item id.
views.grain: one product's receipt within one shipment (one row per ShipmentItem)

views.label: vendors
views.description: One row per supplier: the party that fulfils purchase orders and receives vendor returns, with the trading terms the shop holds with them (account number, price level, purchasing currency) and the catalogue-sync behaviour switches. This is a small reference list, NOT a spend table — order counts, spend and lead times all come from ls_purchase_orders. It is also not a contacts table: people, addresses and reps sit behind relations.
views.grain: one supplier the account buys from

views.label: vendor returns
views.description: One row per return of stock BACK TO a supplier — warranty batches, faulty goods, agreed stock swaps — with the cost value the shop expects to be credited. Header only. It is NOT a customer refund (those are negative sales in the commerce domain) and it is NOT itemised here: the ground-truth documentation exposes the VendorReturnItems relation but none of its member fields, so per-item return quantities are not queryable from this layer.
views.grain: one vendor return document raised at one shop for one vendor

views.label: customers
views.description: The CRM master record: names, company/tax identifiers, date of birth, archive state, and the foreign keys that drive register behaviour (customer type, discount, tax category, store credit account). It is NOT a de-duplicated person table and NOT a purchase-history table: one human commonly owns several customer rows, and walk-in sales carry no customer at all. Contact details (email/phone/address/opt-outs) live in ls_contacts and its child tables, reached via contact_id.
views.grain: one row per Customer record (one POS customer identity, account-wide, not one human being)

views.label: contacts
views.description: The shared contact block: exactly one postal address plus the three marketing opt-out flags, and the parent of the multi-valued email, phone and website child tables. Documented as at most one address per contact, so address lines are flattened here legitimately. This is NOT a per-person table — the same human's several customer records each carry their own contact block, and a ShipTo contact is a delivery destination that may name someone else entirely.
views.grain: one row per Contact record (the single contact block attached to a Customer, CreditAccount or ShipTo)

views.label: contact emails
views.description: The multi-valued email addresses of a contact, one row each, with the documented Primary/Secondary use type. Exists as its own table because a contact can hold several addresses; flattening them onto the customer would silently pick one and hide the rest. It is NOT a consent table — the opt-out flag lives on ls_contacts.no_email.
views.grain: one row per email address held on a contact

views.label: contact phones
views.description: The multi-valued phone numbers of a contact, one row each, tagged with the documented Home/Work/Mobile/Pager/Fax use type. Its own table because contacts routinely hold two or three numbers. It carries no consent: call/SMS permission is ls_contacts.no_phone.
views.grain: one row per phone number held on a contact

views.label: contact websites
views.description: The multi-valued website URLs attached to a contact. Almost always empty for retail consumers and populated only for business accounts. Separate table purely because the container is an array; there is no use-type or label on a website entry.
views.grain: one row per website URL held on a contact

views.label: customer types
views.description: Lookup of customer segments such as VIP, Club, Wholesale or Staff. Attaching a customer of a given type at the register automatically applies that type's discount and tax category, which is how club and staff pricing is actually implemented. It is a definition table only: it holds no customer counts and no revenue.
views.grain: one row per customer type (segment definition)

views.label: credit accounts
views.description: Two different instruments share this endpoint and this table. Customer accounts (gift_card = false) carry a running balance of money owed to the store or held on deposit for a customer. Gift cards (gift_card = true) are bearer instruments with a scannable code, remaining value and no customer link. The balance column is a CURRENT snapshot, not a transaction ledger — the movements themselves are SalePayment records in the payments domain.
views.grain: one row per credit account: either a customer store account or a gift card

views.label: ship tos
views.description: The store's shipping queue and history: a record is created when a sale has to be shipped to the customer, carrying the recipient name, a free-text note, the shipped flag and the destination address via the Contact relation. It is a fulfilment tracker, not a carrier integration — there is no tracking number, carrier, cost or dispatch timestamp anywhere in the object.
views.grain: one row per ShipTo record (one shipment destination created for a sale that needs sending)

views.label: custom fields
views.description: The schema for store-defined customer attributes: name, data type, units, rounding precision, archive state and default value. It defines what CAN be recorded; the values actually recorded live in ls_customer_custom_field_values and the picklist options in ls_custom_field_choices. Reading a value without its definition here is how numbers get misparsed.
views.grain: one row per custom field definition available on customers

views.label: custom field choices
views.description: The picklist options behind choice-typed custom fields: the option's id, its display name, an optional distinct stored value, and whether it can still be deleted. Required to translate a stored customFieldChoiceID into something a human recognises. Only choice-typed fields have rows here.
views.grain: one row per selectable option on a single_choice or multi_choice custom field

views.label: customer custom field values
views.description: The store-defined attributes actually recorded against customers: one row per (customer, custom field) pair, carrying the value plus a snapshot of the field's name and type at read time. This is where segmentation data that has no first-class API field lives (membership numbers, referral source, bike serial, club). Values are untyped in transport, so the type column governs how each one must be parsed.
views.grain: one row per custom field value recorded on one customer

views.label: customer notes
views.description: Free-text notes staff attach to a customer record, with a flag controlling whether the text is printed on receipts. Available on the Customer endpoint through the Note relation. Purely qualitative: it holds no structure, no author and no category, so it supports lookup and text search but not measurement.
views.grain: one row per note attached to a customer

views.label: workorders
views.description: The header of a workshop job: who it is for, which item is being worked on, where it is in the shop's status pipeline, when it came in and when it was promised. It carries NO money of its own — every charge lives in ls_workorder_lines (labour/tasks) or ls_workorder_items (parts), and recognised revenue only exists once the job is checked out into a Sale (sale_id). This is NOT a sales table, NOT a time-clock table, and NOT a history table: status and archived are overwritten in place, so there is no record of what the board looked like last week.
views.grain: one row per workorder — one service/repair ticket for one customer item (a Serialized entry) at one shop

views.label: workorder lines
views.description: The work itself: each task performed or to be performed on a job, with its price, time estimate, assigned employee and done flag. Lightspeed routes a charge here rather than to ls_workorder_items when the underlying Item is type Non-Inventory with TaxClass 'Labor' — that routing rule, not the user, decides which table a charge lands in. These are quoted charges on a job sheet, not recognised revenue, and the hours/minutes here are shop estimates, not a payroll time clock.
views.grain: one row per labour task or misc (non-part) charge on one workorder

views.label: workorder items
views.description: The physical goods consumed on a job: tubes, chains, cables, cassettes. One row per part line on the job sheet, with the quoted retail price, quantity and the special-order flag. Charges land here rather than on ls_workorder_lines whenever the underlying Item is a normal inventory product (labour is a Non-Inventory item with TaxClass 'Labor' and goes to the lines table). Quoted charges only — no cost, no tax amount, and no stock movement happens until checkout.
views.grain: one row per part/product charge on one workorder

views.label: workorder statuses
views.description: The lookup for the workshop pipeline: every status a job can be in, including system states and merchant-defined boards. Read it BEFORE writing any status filter because display names are free text while system_value is the more stable cross-account field. It defines the pipeline; it holds no jobs, dates or money.
views.grain: one row per workorder status configured on the account (system-defined and store-created)

views.label: workorder images
views.description: Reference photos attached to a job — damage on intake, before/after shots, a picture of the serial plate. Metadata only: the row records the filename, CDN pointers, ordering and size, never the image bytes. Useful for evidencing intake condition and for finding jobs with (or without) photographic documentation; it carries no money, no status and no bearing on charges.
views.grain: one row per image attached to one workorder

views.label: shops
views.description: The physical store locations on the account. A Shop owns the Registers inside it, the Sales rung through those registers, its own per-shop inventory quantities and Orders, and it carries the location-level defaults: timezone, workshop labour rate, default sales-tax category and default price level. This is NOT a stock bucket in its own right (per-shop quantities live on ItemShop in the inventory domain) and it is NOT a legal entity (that is the Account).
views.grain: one row per shop (physical store location) on the account, including archived ones

views.label: registers
views.description: A Register is a single point of sale -- a place where money is received -- and each register keeps a separate cash count per payment type. This table is the lookup behind sale.registerID plus the LIVE open/closed state of each till right now. It is NOT a history of till sessions: past opens and closes live on RegisterCount in the cash-management domain.
views.grain: one row per point-of-sale register (till) configured on the account

views.label: employees
views.description: Biographical and account-login information for staff: names, lock-out and archive state, which role (and therefore which rights) they hold, which shop they are restricted to, and a set of live 'currently attached to' pointers. This is the join target for sale.employeeID, workorder staff, register open/close and time-clock entries. It is NOT a payroll record -- Lightspeed stores no pay rate, salary or employment dates anywhere in the API.
views.grain: one row per employee login on the account, including archived former staff

views.label: employee roles
views.description: Named permission roles (e.g. Manager, Sales Associate) that bundle a set of rights and are assigned to employees via Employee.employeeRoleID. A role is a REUSABLE RULE, not a grant: the actual right names it confers are rows in ls_employee_role_rights. Roles have no standalone endpoint -- they are only reachable nested inside the Employee resource.
views.grain: one row per employee role defined on the account

views.label: employee role rights
views.description: The bridge between a role and the individual rights/privileges it confers, exploded from the EmployeeRights collection nested under EmployeeRole. One row means 'this role grants this right'. This is the effective permission set for any employee whose employeeRoleID is set; employees with no role use ls_employee_rights instead.
views.grain: one row per (role, right) grant -- one right conferred by one role

views.label: employee rights
views.description: Per-employee rights, exploded from the EmployeeRights collection nested directly under Employee. These are the fallback permission set: the documentation is explicit that an employee's own rights apply ONLY if employeeRoleID is unset. Same EmployeeRight object as ls_employee_role_rights but a different grain (employee-scoped, not role-scoped), so it is deliberately a separate table.
views.grain: one row per (employee, right) grant made directly to an employee -- effective only when that employee has no role

views.label: employee hours
views.description: Time-clock entries recorded when employees clock in and out of the POS. One row is one shift segment: a check-in, an eventual check-out, the employee and the shop. This is the source for hours-worked and staffing-level questions -- but only for merchants who actually use the Lightspeed time clock. It contains no pay rate, no break tracking, no scheduled/rostered hours and no approval state.
views.grain: one row per clock-in/clock-out entry for one employee at one shop

views.label: session
views.description: Describes the current API session derived from the access token: which employee granted it, which account and API client it belongs to, and a couple of account-wide facts (shop count, linked eCom URL). It is the authoritative source of the accountID that every other R-Series URL needs. It is NOT a login-history table -- there is exactly one row and it reflects the token you are holding right now.
views.grain: one row -- the identity behind the access token currently in use (singleton)

views.label: account
views.description: The merchant account itself: its id, trading name, subscription status, employee licence usage and base currency. This is the legal/billing entity that owns every shop, employee and sale in the layer. WARNING: the V3 documentation publishes NO field table for this object -- every column below is harvested from the documented example payload, so types and null semantics are inferred, not specified.
views.grain: one row -- the Lightspeed Retail (R-Series) account associated with the access token (singleton)

views.label: account purchasing currencies
views.description: The non-base currencies the account is configured to PURCHASE in (i.e. buy stock from overseas suppliers), each with the exchange rate recorded against it. Exploded from the purchasingCurrencies collection in the Account example payload. This is a buying-side configuration list, not a selling-side price list and not a live FX feed.
views.grain: one row per purchasing currency enabled on the account

views.label: locales
views.description: The global list of locales available across Lightspeed and their formatting/currency attributes: currency symbol and code, decimal precision, cash-rounding increment, tax naming, date formats and language tag. This is a GLOBAL reference catalogue -- it lists every locale that exists, not the one this account uses. Which locale an account is on is an account Option, not a field here.
views.grain: one row per locale Lightspeed publishes globally (a global catalogue, not the account's own setting)

views.label: industries
views.description: Lightspeed's built-in retail verticals (Bicycles, Jewelry, Pet, Golf...) and whether each is switched on for this account. Enabling an industry gives the account access to that vertical's shared supplier catalog and its default item templates. Pure configuration reference -- it does not classify products, sales or customers.
views.grain: one row per Lightspeed catalog industry vertical, with its enabled state for this account

views.label: cc gateways
views.description: Legacy per-shop credit-card gateway setup: which processor, its credentials, terminal/market identifiers, enabled and test-mode switches, and the mapping from card brands to PaymentType ids. Documented on the Shop endpoint and only reachable via load_relations=CCGateway. This is CONFIGURATION, not transactions -- no charge, settlement or fee ever appears here, and it holds live credentials.
views.grain: one row per legacy credit-card gateway configuration referenced by a shop

views.label: receipt setups
views.description: Receipt print configuration: the header block, the general footer message, the workorder and credit-card agreement texts, and the logo image with its pixel dimensions. Documented on the Shop endpoint and only reachable via load_relations=ReceiptSetup. Entirely cosmetic -- useful for reproducing a receipt or auditing legal wording, never for analytics.
views.grain: one row per receipt setup configuration referenced by a shop

views.label: currency rates
views.description: Manually maintained foreign-exchange rates used for multi-currency work. One row per currency code, holding the rate of that currency relative to the account's base currency. The documentation is explicit that these rates are NEVER updated automatically -- they are as fresh as the last time a human typed them, so they are a merchant setting, not a market feed.
views.grain: one row per foreign currency exchange rate the merchant maintains

views.label: currency denominations
views.description: The note and coin denominations defined for a locale. This is the reference list the POS uses to build its cash-counting screen, so it is what makes a register count reconcile denomination by denomination. Reference data only: it never changes with trading and carries no money of its own.
views.grain: one physical currency denomination available in a locale

views.label: register counts
views.description: End-of-day (or end-of-shift) till close-out headers. One row per register session: when the till was opened, when it was closed, and which employee did each. This table is the SPINE for cash reconciliation but holds NO money whatsoever — every counted and expected amount lives in ls_register_count_amounts, joined on register_count_id. It is not a list of trading days and not a list of registers.
views.grain: one register close-out — the open-to-close session of a single till, written at the moment the closing count is submitted

views.label: register count amounts
views.description: The per-tender detail of every till close-out: what the system calculated the drawer should hold for a payment type, against what a human physically counted. This is THE source table for cash over/short and drawer-reconciliation questions. It is not a payments table — it never tells you what was sold, only what was in (or supposed to be in) the drawer at close.
views.grain: one payment type's expected-versus-counted pair inside one register close-out

views.label: register withdraws
views.description: Cash moving in and out of a till for reasons other than a sale: opening floats, change top-ups, safe drops and petty-cash payouts. The opening count of a register is stored here as a POSITIVE row, not on the register count. These movements feed the calculated side of ls_register_count_amounts. This is emphatically NOT a sales, payments or refunds table — cash revenue questions belong on the sale-payments table.
views.grain: one cash add or payout at one register (a single signed drawer movement outside of sales)

views.label: register calculated
views.description: The live 'what should be in this drawer right now' figure, broken down per payment type into the payments taken, the cash added and the cash withdrawn since the register was opened. It answers mid-shift questions (is the drawer right now?) that the close-out tables cannot, because they only exist after a count is submitted. It is NOT history: the numbers reset when the register closes, and successive polls supersede rather than accumulate.
views.grain: one payment type's live running total for one register's CURRENTLY OPEN session, as at the instant the endpoint was called

views.label: tax categories
views.description: The account's sales-tax definitions: up to two named component rates plus the tax-inclusive pricing convention. Sales, shops and the TaxesByDay report all point at a row here, and the defaults here may be overridden per tax class in ls_tax_category_classes. This is RATE CONFIGURATION only - it is not tax collected (that is ls_report_taxes_by_day) and it carries no history, so the current row is the only row that ever existed.
views.grain: one sales-tax configuration (TaxCategory, labelled "Sales Tax" in the Lightspeed UI) on the account

views.label: tax category classes
views.description: Rate overrides: the rate a specific tax class attracts under a specific tax category, replacing that category's default tax1_rate/tax2_rate. This is how zero-rated or specially-rated item groups (labour, gift cards, exempt goods) are expressed. A MISSING row means 'use the category default', never 'zero tax' - the distinction is the whole point of the table.
views.grain: one per-tax-class rate override inside one tax category

views.label: tax classes
views.description: Labels that group items for tax treatment (Item, Labor, Gift Card, ...). Items and sale lines carry a tax class, and the accounting reports subtotal by it, which makes this the dimension behind service-vs-goods revenue splits. A tax class is NOT a rate: rates live in ls_tax_categories and ls_tax_category_classes.
views.grain: one tax class label that items and sale lines can carry

views.label: payment types
views.description: The tender methods available at the register (Cash, Credit Card, Gift Card, Credit Account, ...), including their refund routing and whether a customer must be attached. This is the lookup behind SalePayment, RegisterWithdraw, RegisterCount and ls_report_payments_by_day. It is configuration only - no money lives here.
views.grain: one tender method configured on the account

views.label: report payments by day
views.description: Lightspeed-computed daily takings totals by payment type, shop and layaway flag, built for accounting-package export. The canonical source for tender mix over long ranges: one request replaces thousands of raw sale records. It measures MONEY RECEIVED, not revenue recognised, so it will not tie to sale totals.
views.grain: one payment type per shop per day, split by the layaway flag

views.label: report taxes by day
views.description: Lightspeed-computed daily tax totals by tax category and shop, built for accounting-package export and marked read-only in the docs. The canonical source for GST/sales-tax remittance figures over long ranges, and the ONLY source for tax actually collected on a past date - tax rates carry no history, so it cannot be recomputed.
views.grain: one tax category per shop per day

views.label: report discounts by day
views.description: Lightspeed-computed daily discount totals by shop, built for accounting-package export. The cheap way to answer 'how much did we give away' over long ranges without scanning raw sales. Deliberately coarse: there is NO per-discount, per-item or per-staff breakdown here.
views.grain: one shop per day

views.label: report tax class sales by day
views.description: Lightspeed-computed daily sales subtotals broken down by tax class and shop, carrying BOTH a FIFO and an average cost basis for the same goods. Built for accounting-package export. The cheapest route to margin by tax class (service versus retail) over long ranges, and the only place two alternative COGS bases sit side by side.
views.grain: one tax class per shop per day

views.label: report orders by tax class
views.description: Lightspeed-computed accounting report of purchase orders RECEIVED from vendors, broken down per order and subtotaled by tax class, with vendor identification. The cheap way to summarise restocking spend by day, vendor and class over long ranges. Its two shipping/other cost columns are whole-order values repeated on every row, which is what makes the table non-additive as a whole.
views.grain: one tax-class cost subtotal within one received purchase order

views.label: 1099 contacts
views.description: Per-contact 1099 box amounts for a US tax year, exploded from the report's Contacts array: what the org paid each reportable vendor, bucketed into IRS form boxes, plus the identity fields (name, address, TIN) that would print on the form. Amounts are ANNUAL AGGREGATES DERIVED FROM PAYMENTS — never add them to payment- or bill-level cash metrics or the same dollars count twice. Identity fields are a point-in-time snapshot of the contact's W-9 data and are heavily PII.
views.grain: one 1099 summary row per contact per report tax year

views.label: 1099 reports
views.description: Header of the US 1099 report (GET /Reports/TenNinetyNine), fetched once per reportYear the scan iterates. The interesting data is the per-contact box amounts exploded into xero_1099_contacts; this table anchors the year partition and records when Xero last recomputed the report. The report is a LIVE recomputation over the org's payments and 1099 rules, not a frozen filing — re-fetching a past year after bookkeeping changes returns different numbers.
views.grain: one 1099 report header per requested tax year

views.label: accounts
views.description: The org's chart of accounts — the dimension every financial number in the connector eventually joins to. Class (ASSET/LIABILITY/EQUITY vs REVENUE/EXPENSE) is the read-only, authoritative statement split; Type is the granular behavior (BANK, DIRECTCOSTS, OVERHEADS…); SystemAccount marks the control accounts Xero manages itself (DEBTORS = AR control, CREDITORS = AP control, GST = tax control). Archived and deleted accounts remain referenced by historical journal lines, so this dimension must never be pre-filtered to ACTIVE inside a historical join.
views.grain: one chart-of-accounts entry per AccountID

views.label: asset settings
views.description: Per-organisation fixed-asset configuration: register numbering, the date asset depreciation started in Xero, the date depreciation was last run, and the default disposal gain/loss accounts. last_depreciation_date is the freshness bound for every book value in xero_assets — accumulated depreciation and accounting_book_value are computed through that date, not today. opt_in_for_tax records the organisation's tax-depreciation election, but this connector revision exposes no tax book values, so tax-basis questions cannot be answered from staging.
views.grain: one fixed-asset settings record per organisation (unkeyed API singleton)

views.label: asset types
views.description: Depreciation classes that categorise fixed assets and — critically — carry the three GL account mappings that turn depreciation into ledger truth: the fixed-asset cost account, the accumulated-depreciation contra account, and the depreciation-expense P&L account. The embedded BookDepreciationSetting here is only the DEFAULT copied onto an asset at registration; each asset keeps its own overridable copy on xero_assets, so depreciation analytics read the asset's columns, not these defaults. locks marks types with posted accumulated depreciation that Xero refuses to delete; unlocked unused types can hard-delete and vanish between scans.
views.grain: one asset type (depreciation class) per assetTypeId

views.label: assets
views.description: The fixed-asset register: every capitalised asset Xero tracks, with its acquisition cost, its own depreciation policy (flattened from assets:BookDepreciationSetting), Xero-computed depreciation state (flattened from assets:BookDepreciationDetail) and the current accounting net book value. This is the register view, not the ledger: statutory depreciation expense and accumulated-depreciation postings live in journals against the asset type's GL accounts (ledger_config domain). Every book-value and accumulated-depreciation figure is computed only through the organisation's last depreciation run (xero_asset_settings.last_depreciation_date) and is a last-value-over-time snapshot, never a flow. Net-book-value questions filter asset_status = 'Registered': Draft rows have no GL existence yet and Disposed rows carry frozen history.
views.grain: one fixed-asset register entry per assetId (Draft, Registered or Disposed)

views.label: attachments
views.description: Single cross-parent catalog of file attachments across every attachment-capable accounting endpoint (Invoices, CreditNotes, BankTransactions, BankTransfers, Contacts, Accounts, ManualJournals, Receipts, PurchaseOrders, Quotes, RepeatingInvoices...), fetched by per-record fan-out. Rows are file METADATA — the binary lives behind another rate-budgeted call. Because the fan-out burns one request per parent against a hard rate budget, coverage is sampled/limited: a parent with no rows here is 'not scanned or none', never provably 'none'.
views.grain: one attachment on one parent record, keyed by parent endpoint + parent id + attachment id

views.label: bank transaction line item tracking
views.description: Tracking category and option assignments stamped on bank transaction lines — Xero's department/region/cost-centre dimensions applied to directly-coded cash. One row per assignment, at most two per line (one per active tracking category). This is the join path for 'spend by department' over spend/receive money; monetary amounts deliberately stay on the line table so this table never carries money that could double.
views.grain: one tracking category/option assignment on one bank transaction line item

views.label: bank transaction line items
views.description: GL coding detail of each bank transaction: how one cash movement was split across accounts, tax rates, items and (via the tracking child table) departments and regions. 'What did we spend directly-coded cash on' resolves here — but only after joining the parent for direction (type), lifecycle (status) and tax treatment (line_amount_types), none of which exist at line level. Line amounts are unsigned and inherit the parent's currency.
views.grain: one GL coding line per bank transaction, keyed by its zero-based position in the LineItems array

views.label: bank transactions
views.description: The spend-and-receive money ledger of every Xero bank account: cash coded straight to GL accounts rather than applied to an invoice or bill. Only type SPEND and RECEIVE rows are first-class cash here — the RECEIVE-/SPEND-TRANSFER, -PREPAYMENT and -OVERPAYMENT types are bank-side shadows of records whose accounting truth lives in xero_bank_transfers, xero_prepayments and xero_overpayments, and every transfer contributes TWO rows (one leg per account). Invoice and bill payments never appear here at all (they are xero_payments), so this table is not the complete bank feed; the reconcilable per-account cash truth is journal lines on BANK-class accounts. Amounts are unsigned and in currency_code — direction lives entirely in type.
views.grain: one money-in or money-out movement on one Xero bank account per BankTransactionID

views.label: bank transfers
views.description: Movements of funds between two of the organisation's own bank accounts. Each row is the transfer instruction; Xero simultaneously mints a SPEND-TRANSFER bank transaction in the source account and a RECEIVE-TRANSFER in the destination (from_bank_transaction_id / to_bank_transaction_id point at them), so the money in this table always appears twice more in xero_bank_transactions. Transfers relocate cash — they are never income, expense, or a change in total cash, and any flow metric that fails to exclude their legs invents money.
views.grain: one instruction moving funds between two bank accounts of the same organisation per BankTransferID

views.label: batch payments
views.description: Header for a group of bill payments (PAYBATCH) or invoice collections (RECBATCH) that hit the bank as one consolidated transaction. The members are ordinary rows in xero_payments carrying this batch_payment_id, and total_amount equals the sum of those members — so a metric that aggregates both tables counts the same cash twice. This table answers 'what single movements will the bank statement show' and carries the bank-file reference fields; per-document settlement detail always comes from the member payments.
views.grain: one batch payment header per BatchPaymentID, grouping member payments into a single bank movement

views.label: branding themes
views.description: The org's document templates (logo, layout) referenced by invoices, credit notes, quotes and repeating templates via branding_theme_id. A small unpaged config set. Analytically useful because many orgs use themes to separate trading names or brands — making this an accidental business-unit dimension.
views.grain: one branding theme per BrandingThemeID

views.label: budget balances
views.description: The numbers of the planning layer: one row per month bucket ('2019-08') per budgeted account per budget. Modeled as last_value_over_time on the period axis because for balance-sheet accounts the figure is a TARGET BALANCE — summing targets across months double-counts. P&L-account rows are genuinely monthly flows and may be summed across periods, but only after checking the joined account's class; the safe default is to compare period-to-period. Rows arrive via the per-budget fan-out swept over DateFrom/DateTo windows.
views.grain: one budgeted period amount per (budget, account, period)

views.label: budget lines
views.description: The membership bridge between a budget and the chart of accounts: one row per account the budget plans, with the period amounts hanging off xero_budget_balances. Carries no measures itself — its job is to say WHICH accounts a budget covers, and to anchor the (budget, account) key the balances repeat.
views.grain: one budgeted account per (budget, account)

views.label: budget tracking
views.description: The scope declaration of a TRACKING budget: which tracking option (e.g. Region = East) the budget's numbers apply to, up to two pairs per budget mirroring the two-category limit. Empty for OVERALL budgets. To compare a tracking budget against actuals, actuals must be filtered through xero_journal_line_tracking to the SAME option pairs — comparing it to unfiltered actuals understates performance against plan.
views.grain: one tracking category/option pair scoping a budget per (budget, tracking category)

views.label: budgets
views.description: The org's planning layer: the OVERALL budget covers the whole org, while TRACKING budgets re-plan the same org sliced to specific tracking option pairs (see xero_budget_tracking). Budgets are definitions only — the numbers live in xero_budget_lines/xero_budget_balances fetched per budget. Because a tracking budget overlaps the overall one, budget-vs-actual must pick exactly ONE BudgetID per question; summing across budgets counts the same plan twice.
views.grain: one budget definition per BudgetID

views.label: connections
views.description: The authorization roster from the identity API: one row per Xero tenant the user has currently consented to share with Albert. tenant_id is the xero-tenant-id every accounting call is scoped by and the join to xero_organisations. This table defines the sync universe — a tenant that vanishes from it has revoked access, and its staged data freezes at the last successful sync rather than being deleted.
views.grain: one authorized app-to-tenant connection per connection id

views.label: contact addresses
views.description: Typed address slots exploded from the contact record. Xero stores at most one address per type: POBOX is the postal/billing address that prints on documents, STREET is the physical/delivery address — geographic questions must pick the type that matches their intent. Xero pads responses with empty stubs, so a row proves the slot exists, not that an address does.
views.grain: one address per contact per address type (POBOX or STREET)

views.label: contact balances
views.description: Xero's own answer to 'what does this contact owe us, and what do we owe them, right now': outstanding and overdue amounts for accounts receivable (their unpaid sales invoices) and accounts payable (your unpaid bills to them). Amounts are RAW document-currency sums that Xero explicitly does not convert to the base currency, so cross-contact totals are only meaningful in single-currency books. This is a snapshot that each sync overwrites — use it for 'top debtors today', and use invoices or journals for aging, history, or base-currency totals.
views.grain: one current AR/AP balance snapshot per contact, as of the latest sync

views.label: contact cis settings
views.description: Per-contact UK Construction Industry Scheme configuration, fetched by fan-out per contact: whether the contact is a CIS subcontractor and the deduction rate Xero withholds from their payments. Only UK construction orgs have this data at all — for everyone else the endpoint returns nothing, and absence of a row means 'not applicable', never 'not a subcontractor'. The rate is applied at payment time; the actual deducted amounts live on documents, not here.
views.grain: one CIS deduction profile per contact (UK Construction Industry Scheme orgs only)

views.label: contact group members
views.description: The many-to-many bridge between contacts and their groups, exploded from the per-group fan-out fetch — the list endpoint never includes members. Membership is CURRENT-STATE only: Xero silently removes archived and merged contacts from groups and keeps no history, so segment membership cannot be reconstructed for the past. Contacts can belong to many groups at once, which makes every join through this table a deliberate one-to-many fan-out.
views.grain: one membership edge per (contact group, contact) pair

views.label: contact groups
views.description: User-curated contact segments ('VIP', 'Wholesale', 'North region') — the cheapest segmentation dimension Xero offers, maintained by hand in the org. The list endpoint returns only ACTIVE groups and omits members entirely; membership arrives via the per-group fan-out into xero_contact_group_members. No modified watermark exists, so the ingester rescans the (small) set every sync and detects deletions as vanished ids.
views.grain: one contact group per ContactGroupID

views.label: contact persons
views.description: The ADDITIONAL people attached to a contact — the primary person lives on xero_contacts (first_name/last_name/email_address), so a complete people-extract is that record UNION these rows. Xero assigns contact persons no identifier, so rows are keyed by array position, which survives only until someone edits the list. The analytical payload is include_in_emails: it decides who is CC'd on emailed invoices and statements.
views.grain: one additional contact person per contact per array position

views.label: contact phones
views.description: Typed phone slots exploded from the contact record: DEFAULT (what the Xero UI displays), DDI (direct dial), MOBILE, FAX and OFFICE. Xero returns the full slot set padded with blanks, so presence of a row is meaningless — the analytical unit is a non-empty phone_number. A dialable number is the concatenation of country code, area code and number, each optional and inconsistently filled.
views.grain: one phone entry per contact per phone type

views.label: contacts
views.description: The master directory behind every money table: customers, suppliers and everyone in between share this single namespace, distinguished only by the derived is_customer/is_supplier evidence flags. Rows persist through archiving and merging — the scan pages and passes includeArchived=true, so merge losers arrive as ARCHIVED shells whose merged_to_contact_id points at the survivor — which means entity-level analysis must filter contact_status and collapse merges or it overcounts. Almost everything here beyond identity and lifecycle is DEFAULT configuration (tax types, account codes, currency, payment terms, tracking) that seeds NEW documents and proves nothing about historical ones; the document tables carry their own values. Fan-out detail lives in the child tables: xero_contact_persons, xero_contact_addresses, xero_contact_phones, xero_contact_balances, xero_contact_group_members and xero_contact_cis_settings.
views.grain: one Xero contact record per ContactID, including ACTIVE, ARCHIVED, GDPRREQUEST and merged-away records

views.label: credit note allocations
views.description: Application evidence exploded from CreditNote.Allocations: each row spreads part of a credit note's value onto one invoice, reducing that invoice's amount_due without any cash moving. This is the event_link between credit and invoice — revenue impact stays on credit note lines, cash refunds stay in xero_payments. Amounts are in the credit note's currency.
views.grain: one allocation of one credit note against one invoice, per credit note and array position

views.label: credit note line items
views.description: The contra side of xero_invoice_line_items: what was credited back, per product and GL account. Rows are stored positive but reduce revenue (ACCRECCREDIT parent) or spend (ACCPAYCREDIT parent) — netting against invoice lines requires negation. Direction, status, currency and LineAmountTypes all come from the parent xero_credit_notes row.
views.grain: one line item on one credit note per LineItemID

views.label: credit notes
views.description: Negative-document header mirroring xero_invoices: ACCRECCREDIT reduces what a customer owes (contra revenue), ACCPAYCREDIT reduces what the org owes a supplier (contra spend). Net revenue = ACCREC invoices minus ACCRECCREDIT credit notes — adding credit note totals to invoice totals inflates instead of nets. Credit is consumed two ways: allocation against invoices (xero_credit_note_allocations) or cash refund (rows in xero_payments); remaining_credit is what is still unconsumed right now.
views.grain: one credit note document (customer credit ACCRECCREDIT or supplier credit ACCPAYCREDIT) per CreditNoteID

views.label: currencies
views.description: Tiny reference list of the currencies the org has ever enabled — the decode table for every CurrencyCode column in the connector. Presence means 'added to the subscription at some point', not 'currently transacting'; currencies cannot be removed once used, so the list only grows. No watermark and no paging: fully re-scanned each sync.
views.grain: one currency per ISO code enabled in the org's subscription

views.label: expense claim payments
views.description: Reimbursement cash events, exploded from the Payments array embedded in each expense claim. This is their only home in the design: a Payment served by GET /Payments allocates to exactly one invoice, credit note, prepayment or overpayment, and an expense claim is none of those — so these rows reach staging through the claim scan alone, and a 'total cash paid out' built from xero_payments by itself omits employee reimbursements. Amounts are in org base currency (classic claims carry no currency or rate fields). Status DELETED un-pays the claim yet remains in the payload — filter AUTHORISED on every sum.
views.grain: one reimbursement payment applied to one expense claim

views.label: expense claim receipts
views.description: The authoritative claim-to-receipt mapping, exploded from the Receipts array embedded in each expense claim. Receipt bodies land in xero_receipts from their own endpoint; this table is the wiring that says which receipts were submitted on which claim. A receipt belongs to at most one claim, and DRAFT (not-yet-claimed) receipts have no row here — their absence is workflow state, not data loss.
views.grain: one attachment of one receipt to one expense claim

views.label: expense claims
views.description: The reimbursement wrapper of Xero's classic expense-claims workflow: who is owed money, how much is outstanding, and which accounting period it reports under. The claim itself carries no expense categories — GL and merchant detail live on the receipts (xero_receipts / xero_receipt_line_items) linked via xero_expense_claim_receipts. Amounts are always in the org's base currency (classic claims have no currency fields). VOIDED and DELETED claims are still returned by the API and must be excluded from every liability number.
views.grain: one expense claim submitted by one org user for reimbursement

views.label: file associations
views.description: The bridge that turns the file library into audit evidence: each row attaches one file to one business record, addressed by the polymorphic (object_group, object_id) pair. This is how 'which invoices have no supporting document' and 'what paperwork backs this bank transaction' resolve — filter object_group first, then join object_id to that group's table. Rows are gathered by per-file fan-out (one API call per file in xero_files), so the table is availability-optional and can trail the library under the Files API rate budget. Five denormalized fields (file_name, file_size_bytes, file_created_date_utc, association_date_utc, send_with_object) are only returned by the per-object endpoint GET /Associations/{ObjectId} and are NULL under the bulk scan — name/size/created resolve via the xero_files join instead.
views.grain: one row per attachment of one file to one Xero business record — a file attached to N records yields N rows

views.label: files
views.description: The tenant's document library: every file uploaded to or emailed into Xero Files, with content metadata and the uploader's identity flattened from the nested files:User object. It carries no money — its analytical job is evidencing OTHER records, which resolves by joining through xero_file_associations. Documents added straight onto a transaction through the accounting Attachments endpoints are served by xero_attachments (org_meta); treat the two populations as complementary evidence sources, never as duplicates of each other. Deletion is physical and unflagged and the Files API accepts no modified-since filter, so rows reflect the latest full sweep of the library and absence is the only deletion signal.
views.grain: one row per file stored in the tenant's Xero Files library, Inbox included

views.label: folders
views.description: The flat (non-nested) folder structure of the Files library, dominated by one special row: the Inbox, where emailed-in and unfiled documents accumulate until someone files or attaches them. It is the workflow dimension for document hygiene — files whose folder is the Inbox are paperwork awaiting processing. file_count is Xero's own point-in-time tally kept for reconciliation; live counts always come from xero_files.
views.grain: one row per folder in the tenant's Xero Files library, including the system Inbox

views.label: history records
views.description: Single cross-parent audit trail: who did what, when, to which document (created, approved, voided, edited, emailed, notes), fetched by per-record fan-out from GET /{Endpoint}/{Guid}/History. The source rows have NO id and arrive newest-first, so the key is a minted ordinal that is only stable within one sync — order by date_utc, always. Same hard rate budget as attachments, so coverage is sampled and availability is optional.
views.grain: one audit/history event per parent record per array position at sync time

views.label: invoice line items
views.description: The revenue and spend fact at its true grain: what was billed, for which product/service, posted to which GL account, carrying which tracking dimensions. Rows inherit direction (ACCREC vs ACCPAY), status, currency and LineAmountTypes from the parent — this table alone cannot tell a sale from a bill, so every aggregate joins xero_invoices. line_amount is net of discounts, and whether it includes tax depends on the parent's line_amount_types.
views.grain: one line item on one invoice or bill per LineItemID

views.label: invoice reminders
views.description: Org-level toggle from GET /InvoiceReminders/Settings: whether Xero's automatic invoice reminder emails are switched on. A single-row config table; the API exposes only the on/off flag, not the per-reminder schedule visible in the Xero UI. Useful context when interpreting collections behaviour — an org with reminders off is chasing debt manually.
views.grain: one invoice-reminder settings record per organisation

views.label: invoices
views.description: Document-header fact for BOTH sides of the ledger: one Xero Invoice object is a sales invoice (Type=ACCREC, money owed to the org) or a supplier bill (Type=ACCPAY, money the org owes). Header totals (sub_total/total_tax/total) are normalized and safe to aggregate after filtering type and status; line-level revenue analysis belongs on xero_invoice_line_items. VOIDED and DELETED documents are still returned by the API and still land here — every total must exclude them. Settlement state (amount_due/amount_paid/amount_credited) is current-state only: it reflects now, not any historical point in time.
views.grain: one invoice document (sales invoice ACCREC or bill ACCPAY) per InvoiceID

views.label: items
views.description: The product/service dimension and the only inventory-balance surface in the accounting API. Document lines reference items by user-editable code (item_code), not by uuid — so this table joins to facts through `code`. Sales/purchase details are DEFAULTS offered in the Xero UI, not transacted prices; the transacted price is always unit_amount on the document line. is_tracked_as_inventory gates the stock story: only tracked items carry quantity_on_hand and total_cost_pool (average-cost value of stock), and both are point-in-time snapshots as of the last sync — Xero exposes no stock history. Those two balance columns are why this table is typed last_value_over_time rather than reference: every other column is catalog configuration, but stock value and quantity are as-at balances that may be summed across items and never across time. Items hard-delete: rows vanish from the API and are tombstoned only by full identity scans.
views.grain: one product or service item in the org's catalog, identified by ItemID

views.label: journal line tracking
views.description: How the org's analysis dimensions (Department, Region…) attach to the statutory ledger: each row pins one journal line to one option of one tracking category. This is the join that turns P&L into P&L-by-department — filter or group ledger lines through it. Lines with no tracking simply have no rows here, so segment reports silently exclude untracked activity unless you LEFT JOIN and bucket the NULLs as 'unassigned'.
views.grain: one tracking category/option pair applied to one journal line (at most two pairs per line)

views.label: journal lines
views.description: The atoms of the statutory ledger: balanced debit/credit lines, ALWAYS in the org's base currency regardless of the source document's currency — the one place in Xero where summing across records is currency-safe without conversion. NetAmount is signed (positive = debit, negative = credit) and sums to zero within every journal; P&L, trial-balance and balance-sheet answers are SUM(net_amount) sliced by the joined account's Class from xero_accounts. Inherits the Advanced journals scope gate from the parent scan.
views.grain: one signed debit or credit ledger line per JournalLineID (a globally unique uuid)

views.label: journals
views.description: The statutory general ledger feed: every posted transaction in Xero — invoices, payments, bank lines, payroll, manual journals — becomes exactly one immutable journal header whose lines are always in the org's base currency. Because the Reports endpoints are scope-refused, this is the ONLY path to P&L, trial-balance and balance-sheet answers. The endpoint sits behind Xero's Advanced-tier accounting.journals.read approval, so availability is optional: when the scope is missing, financial-statement answers must degrade explicitly, never silently substitute invoice totals.
